**LONDON, England (CNN)** — A team of visionary engineering students behind an autonomous "thinking" yacht is aiming to break a world record by navigating the vessel across the Atlantic Ocean entirely without human assistance. 

The four-meter vessel, named *Avalon*, was designed and constructed by an eight-member team of third-year students at the Swiss science university ETH Zurich, competing under the banner "Students Sailing Autonomously" (SSA). Before its initial launch, the yacht was hoisted to have its keel secured in place.

The team plans to enter *Avalon* into a robotic sailing regatta in July before embarking on the Microtransat Transatlantic Challenge in early September. Utilizing specialized sensors to monitor wind speed and direction, the vessel is programmed to navigate toward designated coordinates by dynamically adapting its course and sails to changing atmospheric conditions.

Hendrik Erckens, one of the SSA project managers, told CNN that a successful voyage would mark the first time an unmanned vessel has ever completed the crossing, setting a landmark world record. The voyage is scheduled to begin off the western coast of Ireland and conclude in the Caribbean.

"For us, the Microtransat challenge is the ultimate goal, and I am quite confident we can achieve it," Erckens said. "During this week's trials, the boat has performed precisely as intended, and it is completely watertight. Over the past few days, we successfully executed autonomous tacks and jibes, and we are now testing its navigation capabilities."

Having initiated the project in September 2008, the team has progressed from initial design and construction to comprehensive on-water testing.

Although the team will track *Avalon’s* position via an onboard Global Positioning System (GPS), Erckens emphasized that they will have no manual control over the vessel once the challenge begins.

"We will launch it, and it will operate completely autonomously," Erckens explained. "It features stern-mounted solar cells for power, alongside auxiliary energy supplies. An onboard satellite communication system also allows the vessel to independently download weather forecasts and calculate the optimal route."

Erckens expressed confidence that the vessel's carbon-fiber hull will withstand the turbulent Atlantic seas—a formidable obstacle that has thwarted numerous manned expeditions, including Sir Richard Branson’s attempt to break the transatlantic speed record aboard the 99-foot *Virgin Money* last autumn.

"We feel our primary advantage over other teams is our background as mechanical engineers," Erckens noted. "We designed this boat ourselves, tailored specifically for this objective."

Beyond the competition, Erckens believes the technology could eventually yield a next-generation autopilot system for larger commercial and recreational yachts. "While commercially available autopilots currently only control the rudder, our system is designed to manage the sails as well," he said.

A team of ambitious Swiss engineering students has unveiled a cutting-edge maritime project: **Avalon**, a four-meter autonomous yacht designed to navigate the open ocean entirely on its own. Built to push the boundaries of modern robotic navigation, the unmanned boat is engineered to operate continuously without any human intervention.

### Advanced Engineering on the High Seas
At the heart of Avalon’s design is a sophisticated, self-sustaining system capable of braving harsh marine environments. Measuring four meters in length, the vessel is powered by onboard solar panels, which supply clean energy to its core electronics and propulsion systems. Avalon relies on an array of advanced sensors and GPS technology to analyze its surroundings, monitor ocean conditions, and plot optimal routes in real time. This allows the yacht to make complex navigational decisions independently, eliminating the need for remote control or a human crew.

### The Ultimate Test: Crossing the Atlantic
The Swiss team has set its sights on an extraordinary milestone for their creation. This coming September, they plan to enter Avalon into the prestigious **Microtransat Transatlantic Challenge**. The grueling route will see the vessel set sail from the coast of Ireland and navigate thousands of miles across the open ocean to its destination in the Caribbean. 

The stakes for the mission could not be higher. If Avalon reaches the Caribbean successfully, the project will achieve a historic breakthrough, setting a new world record for the longest journey completed by an unmanned vessel.

### Rigorous Preparation
Before launching into the Atlantic, the team is leaving nothing to chance. Avalon is currently undergoing extensive on-water testing to ensure every system is ocean-ready. Engineers are carefully evaluating the vessel's hull for complete watertightness while fine-tuning its complex navigation algorithms. These trials are critical for validating the yacht’s autonomous maneuvers, ensuring it can safely handle unpredictable weather, strong currents, and potential sea obstacles.

As September approaches, final adjustments are being made to turn this ambitious vision into a reality. A successful crossing by Avalon would not only secure a world record for the student team but could also pave the way for the future of sustainable, unmanned oceanographic research.

counterfactuals.output:
**ZURICH (CNN)** — The Atlantic Ocean has humbled seasoned ocean racers, massive cargo ships, and legendary explorers. Now, an eight-student team from Switzerland is hoping a four-meter robotic sailboat can succeed where so many others have failed.

The engineering students from ETH Zurich have spent thousands of hours designing and building "Avalon," a state-of-the-art autonomous vessel. Their goal? To conquer the Microtransat Challenge, an international competition that tasks unmanned boats with navigating nearly 3,000 miles of open ocean completely unassisted.

For the team, the project is a high-stakes blend of robotics, oceanography, and sheer grit.

"The ocean is completely relentless," Hendrik Erckens, the project’s team manager, told CNN. "When you put a four-meter boat in the middle of the Atlantic, you are fighting massive waves, strong currents, and unpredictable weather—all without a human on board to make quick fixes."

### A robot built for the high seas

Avalon is not a typical RC boat. Measuring just under 13 feet, the sleek vessel features a lightweight carbon-fiber hull, a rigid wingsail for propulsion, and an array of solar panels powering its internal computers. 

Because human intervention is strictly forbidden during the Microtransat, Avalon’s brain—a complex suite of custom software and sensors—must make every tactical decision on its own. The boat constantly analyzes wind direction, GPS coordinates, and weather forecasts to plot its route, dodging shipping traffic and storms along the way.

The Microtransat Challenge, launched in 2005 to stimulate research in autonomous ocean navigation, has proven to be notoriously difficult. Dozens of teams from prestigious universities and research institutions around the world have attempted the crossing; only a handful have ever completed it. Most vessels founder due to mechanical failure, power loss, or collision with sea debris.

Erckens and his team are acutely aware of the odds stacked against them.

"We are just eight students, but we’ve built something that has to survive conditions that can sink massive ships," Erckens said. "Every single line of code, every line of software, and every seal on the hull had to be perfect. One small leak or one logic loop in the code, and the mission is over."

### The ultimate test

To prepare for the grueling voyage, the ETH Zurich team put Avalon through rigorous testing in Swiss lakes and off the coast of Western Europe. They simulated catastrophic failures—such as loss of satellite connection or sudden gear breakdowns—to ensure the boat’s autonomous systems could recover on their own.

Beyond the academic achievement, the team hopes the technology developed for Avalon could have real-world applications, such as low-cost ocean data collection, environmental monitoring, or search-and-rescue operations. 

As the launch window approaches, the atmosphere among the team is a mix of exhaustion, pride, and nervous anticipation. 

"Once we push Avalon into the water and watch it steer away from the coast, it’s completely out of our hands," Erckens reflected. "It’s a bit terrifying, to be honest. But it’s also the ultimate test of everything we’ve worked for over the past year. Now we just have to trust the boat."

If Avalon successfully reaches the other side of the Atlantic, Erckens and his seven teammates won't just win a trophy—they will join an elite group of pioneers pushing the boundaries of autonomous technology on the high seas.

**ST. JOHN’S, Newfoundland** — A team of student engineers from the Pacific Institute of Technology launched a groundbreaking attempt to make history on Tuesday, deploying a 12-foot, fully autonomous sailboat into the freezing waters of the North Atlantic. 

The unmanned vessel, named *Aura-1*, is attempting to set a world record by becoming the fastest robotic boat to cross the Atlantic Ocean entirely without human control or remote intervention. 

Powered by solar panels and guided by advanced machine-learning algorithms, *Aura-1* is designed to make its own navigational decisions over the 3,000-mile journey to the coast of Ireland. The vessel relies on a suite of sensors to monitor weather patterns, adjust its carbon-fiber wing sail, and detect incoming maritime traffic to avoid collisions.

"We’ve spent three years preparing for the absolute worst the ocean can throw at us," said Maya Lin, a senior robotics student and project lead. "Once *Aura-1* leaves the coast, there is no joystick, no pilot, and no second chance. The boat has to think for itself."

Crossing the Atlantic has proven notoriously difficult for autonomous surface vehicles. Previous international attempts have been cut short by severe storms, equipment failure, and even shark attacks. To withstand the harsh ocean environment, the team reinforced the hull with high-strength Kevlar and built redundant backup systems for all critical electronics. 

Beyond setting a world record, the mission carries a scientific purpose. *Aura-1* is equipped with oceanographic sensors that will gather real-time data on surface water temperatures, ocean acidity, and microplastic concentration, beaming the information back to the university via satellite.

If successful, the vessel is expected to complete its journey in roughly 20 to 25 days, landing near the coast of Galway, Ireland. 

The public can follow *Aura-1*’s real-time position, speed, and ocean data through the project’s live satellite tracking website.

**GHOST IN THE RIGGING: SWISS ENGINEERS BUILD ‘AVALON,’ THE AUTONOMOUS YACHT THAT THINKS IN KNOTS**

**By Julian Vance**  
*Senior Tech & Mobility Correspondent*  
**ZURICH —** 

To a veteran sailor, trimming a canvas sail is an intuitive art form. It is the sensory alchemy of feeling the breeze on the back of your neck, reading the micro-ripples on the water’s surface, and adjusting a winch by a fraction of an inch to wring half a knot more speed out of the wind.

To a team of Swiss engineering students, however, that art form is simply a high-dimensional math problem waiting to be solved. 

Meet *Avalon*, a sleek, carbon-fibre unmanned sailing vessel designed to conquer one of the final frontiers of autonomous mobility: the unpredictable, friction-heavy world of open-ocean sailing. Developed by a cross-disciplinary team of student researchers in Switzerland, *Avalon* isn't just a remote-controlled boat. It is a fully autonomous, self-correcting "thinking yacht" capable of navigating complex sea routes and adjusting its own sails without a single human finger on the tiller.

### Carbon-Fibre and Code

At first glance, *Avalon* looks less like a traditional sailboat and more like a piece of aerospace technology that fell into the water. Its minimalist, ultra-light carbon-fibre hull glistens under the Swiss sun, designed for maximum hydrodynamic efficiency and structural resilience against punishing swells. 

But the true magic lies beneath the composite deck. 

While autonomous cars rely on lanes, GPS, and predictable asphalt, autonomous sailing vessels face a dynamic, multi-axis fluid dynamics puzzle. The wind changes direction in milliseconds; waves push the hull off-course; currents drag from below. 

To solve this, the Swiss team equipped *Avalon* with an array of industrial-grade sensor suites: solid-state ultrasonic anemometers to measure wind vector and velocity, high-frequency IMUs (Inertial Measurement Units) to track pitch, roll, and yaw, and dual-antenna GPS for sub-meter positioning. 

All of this data feeds into *Avalon’s* central processor—the vessel’s digital brain.

```
       [ WIND & WAVE SENSORS ] 
                 │
                 ▼
     [ REAL-TIME AI BRAIN ] ──(Calculates optimal attack angle)
                 │
                 ▼
[ AUTOMATED WINCHES & STEERING ] ──(Adjusts sails & rudder in ms)
```

"Road vehicles mainly deal with two dimensions," explains continuous-control team lead Lukas Meier during a demonstration at Lake Zurich. "A sailing yacht operates in a constantly shifting medium where the propulsion source—the wind—is also the primary destabilizing force. *Avalon* has to constantly predict what the environment will do three seconds from now and re-trim its rigging before the wave even hits."

### The Art of Automated Sail Control

The standout innovation of the *Avalon* project is its custom-built automated sail-trimming architecture. 

In a traditional setup, sailors manually pull ropes (sheets) to adjust the angle of the sail relative to the wind. *Avalon* replaces muscle with high-torque, waterproof electric actuators driven by custom reinforcement-learning algorithms. 

The onboard system continuously calculates the "polar code" of the boat—the theoretical maximum speed for any given wind angle—and continuously adjusts the mainsail and jib to hit that peak efficiency. If a sudden gust threatens to capsize the vessel, the control loop detects the heel angle spike and releases the sheets within milliseconds, spilling the wind safer and faster than human reaction times allow.

Navigation is equally sophisticated. Rather than simply plotting a straight line from Point A to Point B, *Avalon’s* pathfinding software continuously executes real-time tacking and gybing calculations. It balances the shortest physical distance against the optimal wind angle, dynamically routing itself around low-pressure zones and dead calms.

### From Student Project to Maritime Revolution

While *Avalon* was born out of academic curiosity and the spirit of competitive robotics—targeting international autonomous micro-rig challenges—its implications stretch far beyond student trophies.

The global maritime industry is currently under immense pressure to decarbonize. Commercial shipping accounts for nearly 3% of global greenhouse gas emissions. While zero-emission cargo ships powered by giant autonomous kites or rigid wings are still in their infancy, the control systems honed by projects like *Avalon* provide the foundational software for that green future.

"What these students are building in miniature is the exact control software commercial shipping will need in ten years," says Dr. Elena Rostova, a marine robotics analyst not affiliated with the project. "Wind-assisted propulsion is returning to global shipping, but commercial crews don't know how to sail giant wind-rigs anymore. You need computers to do it automatically. *Avalon* proves that automated fluid dynamic management works at scale."

### The Horizon

Back on the shores of the lake, the team is prepping *Avalon* for its next major milestone: a continuous, multi-day endurance test designed to push its battery systems, solar recharging arrays, and fail-safe protocols to their limits. 

As the Swiss team releases the carbon-fibre vessel from the dock, there is no captain at the wheel, no crew hauling lines, and no remote control in hand. *Avalon* pauses for a fraction of a second, senses the breeze coming off the Alps, sheets in its mainsail with a faint mechanical hum, and carves a crisp, quiet line through the water.

The era of the thinking ship has officially arrived—and it speaks fluent Swiss engineering.

Here is a detailed overview of the **Autonomous Yacht "Avalon"** project, developed by students at ETH Zurich:

---

### **Project Overview: Autonomous Yacht "Avalon"**

**Avalon** was a groundbreaking robotic sailboat designed, built, and operated by an interdisciplinary team of engineering students from **ETH Zurich** under the Swiss Student Sailing Association (SSA) / ETH Sailing Team. 

The primary goal of the project was to create an uncrewed, fully autonomous sailboat capable of navigating harsh oceanic environments without human intervention.

---

### **1. Key Objectives**
* **The Microtransat Challenge:** The primary target for Avalon was to compete in the *Microtransat Challenge*—a transatlantic race for fully autonomous boats, aiming to cross from Europe (Ireland) to North America/the Caribbean.
* **Engineering Research:** To push the boundaries of marine robotics, renewable power management, real-time path planning, and harsh-weather durability.

---

### **2. Technical Specifications**

* **Dimensions & Hull:** 
  * **Length:** ~3.95 meters (13 feet)
  * **Weight:** ~450 kg (heavily ballasted to ensure self-righting capabilities in extreme waves).
  * **Hull Design:** Monohull optimized for hydrodynamic efficiency and extreme ocean stability.
* **Power Supply:** 
  * **Solar Panels:** Integrated into the deck to charge onboard batteries.
  * **Methanol Fuel Cell:** Used as a backup energy source during prolonged overcast weather or high power consumption.
* **Sensors & Navigation:**
  * GPS, digital compass, wind speed/direction sensors, and tilt/attitude sensors.
  * Satellite communication (Iridium) for transmitting telemetry data back to the ETH Zurich ground team.
* **Control System:**
  * Onboard embedded computers running custom algorithms for path planning, tacking/jibing strategy, obstacle avoidance, and energy management.

---

### **3. The 2009 Transatlantic Mission**

* **Launch:** In December 2009, Avalon was launched from the coast of Ireland into the North Atlantic Ocean.
* **Performance:** The boat successfully navigated hundreds of nautical miles completely autonomously, adjusting its sails and rudder to cope with shifting winds and heavy sea states.
* **Outcome:** After several days at sea and traveling over 300 nautical miles, Avalon encountered severe storms and technical issues (a rudder/actuator malfunction), leading to a loss of steering control. Despite the mission ending prematurely, it set a milestone for distance traveled by an autonomous sailboat at the time.

---

### **4. Impact and Legacy**

* **Pioneer in Marine Robotics:** Avalon was one of the earliest high-profile student-led projects to demonstrate that small, autonomous sailing craft could survive the open ocean.
* **Educational Value:** The project provided hands-on experience in mechatronic integration, control systems, and naval architecture for dozens of ETH Zurich students.
* **Foundation for Future Projects:** The technologies and lessons learned from Avalon laid the foundation for subsequent autonomous vessel research, weather-monitoring buoys, and clean ocean technology initiatives developed at ETH Zurich.
